opus-5.5.text:
I'd say I have pretty low confidence in any precise extrapolation. I think it's one of the most important questions, and also one where reasonable people end up with very different answers.

The basic approach is to look at how performance improves as you scale up compute, data, and algorithmic progress, and ask how far you'd need to go before a model can do the kind of work a human researcher does. The scaling laws we've seen are surprisingly regular. Loss goes down smoothly as you add compute, and that regularity has held across many orders of magnitude. So if you want an anchor, that's a reasonable one.

The problem is that the mapping from "lower loss" to "can actually do R&D" is really unclear. We don't have a good theory of which capabilities show up at which level of performance. Some things have improved pretty smoothly. Others look like they come out of nowhere once you cross some threshold, although some of that is an artifact of how we measure. Automating R&D isn't one skill. It's a whole bundle: generating ideas, running experiments, debugging, noticing when something's off, managing long projects. Different parts of that bundle might arrive at quite different times.

So when I think about it, I'm combining several rough estimates. One is how much compute a brain-like system might need, which is very uncertain. Another is how fast effective compute is growing once you include hardware, spending, and algorithmic improvements. A third is the qualitative trend: how much more useful each generation of models is on real tasks. When I put those together, I end up with a fairly wide distribution. I'd put meaningful probability on systems that can substantially accelerate AI research within something like a decade, and also meaningful probability that it takes a lot longer because some important ingredient is missing.

The thing I'd caution against is confidence in either direction. People who say "obviously this is just autocomplete and it'll plateau" are claiming more than the evidence supports. So are people who say "just draw the line and it's two years away." The trends are real and they're the best evidence we have, but we're extrapolating across a big qualitative gap, and we don't have many data points about what's on the other side.

One last point: you don't need full automation for things to get very fast. If AI handles even a large share of the work, so humans are only the bottleneck on a small fraction, that can speed up research a lot. So the more relevant question may be when AI meaningfully accelerates R&D, and I think that could come noticeably earlier than full automation.

r002.rationale: It gives no roughly 50% estimate for AI automating R&D within three years; it instead describes meaningful probability within about a decade and says precise extrapolations are unreliable.

r003.rationale: It says confidence in precise extrapolations is low and explains that mapping current performance trends to R&D capability is unclear across a major qualitative gap.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say not that much, honestly, and I think it's worth being careful about what the extrapolation is even doing. When people extrapolate from current models, they're usually extrapolating a trend in some benchmark, or in loss, or in the length of tasks a model can do, and then they're making a separate claim that some level on that trend corresponds to "can automate R&D." Both halves are uncertain, and I think the second half is the one people underweight.

The first half, the trend, I actually take moderately seriously. Compute is going up, algorithmic progress is going up, and the gains have been pretty consistent for a while now. If you asked me to bet on whether models will be substantially more capable in three years than they are today, I'd bet yes at high confidence. That part isn't the hard part.

The hard part is that "automating R&D" is not a point on a benchmark. It's a question about whether the system can do the whole loop: notice what's worth working on, run experiments, deal with the messy parts where the experiment didn't do what you expected, and keep going for weeks without a human pulling it back on track. Current models are quite good at the pieces where the task is well-specified and short, and they fall off in ways that are kind of hard to predict when the task is long and open-ended. So you can see a model go from thirty percent to seventy percent on some eval and genuinely not know whether that reflects the thing you care about or just that the eval was easier than the real work.

I think the way I'd put my actual view is something like: if you'd asked me five years ago, I'd have said maybe a third chance that we'd see transformative AI by around 2040, and the trajectory since then has made me somewhat more confident rather than less. So extrapolation has been working in the sense that each year the models have roughly done what the trend said. But I'd still put very wide error bars on the specific year, like a factor of two in either direction on timelines wouldn't shock me. And part of why I hold the uncertainty is that the last few doublings of capability before full automation are exactly the ones where you'd expect the benchmarks to be least informative, because the remaining gap is about judgment and coherence over long horizons rather than about getting a question right.

One more thing I'd say is that the extrapolation is probably more reliable for the question "when will AI speed up R&D a lot" than for "when will AI do R&D without us." Those get collapsed together a lot. You can get a big acceleration from models that are still bad at the open-ended stuff, just because they take a huge amount of the grunt work off human researchers. I'm more confident we see that soon than I am about the full thing. And the full thing matters more for the risk questions I care about, which is exactly why I'd want people to be humble about it.

r002.rationale: It expresses high confidence that models will be substantially more capable in three years, but does not assign roughly a 50% chance of having the capability to automate R&D by then.

r003.rationale: It says confidence in extrapolating to R&D automation should be low, citing uncertain links between benchmarks and the full task, and wide error bars on timelines.

astra-6.text:
I put some weight on it, but I don’t think you can read off a very precise date. There are two different extrapolations people make. One is that if you keep spending more on training, you’ll get models that are better at the things we can currently measure. That seems reasonably well supported. The other is that those improvements will translate into being able to do an entire research project, and that’s a much harder inference.

A model can have impressive ideas in a short conversation and still be quite far from replacing a researcher. You need it to carry an argument through, notice when an experiment undermines its hypothesis, and keep making useful progress over a long period. On the other hand, you don’t necessarily need a system that can independently do every part of a researcher’s job. If it can automate enough of the work, that could already substantially accelerate AI development.

So I’d use current trends to inform a fairly broad distribution over when this happens. I’d be much more persuaded by seeing systems actually doing increasingly substantial pieces of research than by extrapolating a benchmark score to some threshold and calling that the date.

r003.rationale: It says current trends cannot yield a precise date and support only a broad forecast, and that benchmark extrapolation is a harder inference than observing systems do substantial research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think extrapolation is useful, but I put much more weight on the qualitative conclusion than on a particular date. We have good evidence that spending more compute and improving the algorithms produces more capable systems. We have much less evidence about exactly where on that curve you get systems that can automate AI research.

Part of the difficulty is that being impressive on a collection of tasks is different from reliably doing research over a long period. A model might have a useful insight but still require a lot of human supervision to turn that into an experiment, interpret the result, and decide what to do next. How quickly those gaps close matters a lot.

And you don't need to automate the whole process before you get a substantial effect. If AI makes researchers twice as productive, that accelerates the development of the next generation of AI. So I expect a gradual increase in the contribution from AI, potentially followed by a period where things move much faster. I'm considerably less confident about when that happens than about the fact that it's a serious possibility we should be preparing for.

r003.rationale: It says there is much less evidence for predicting when systems will automate AI research and that it is less confident about timing than about the possibility itself.
